Reading

The innocent reading first. The Overview says who built the model, on what, by what method, how accurate it is and what it found, then gives the reception, from the article and its press.

Findings
  • THE STUDY HELD. 'The model was trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples', 'Bayesian ridge regression', 'a mean absolute error of roughly 28 to 31 years', '79% of its estimates for 135 undated scrolls aligned realistically with human paleographic evaluations': the record's 24 samples, its 27.9 to 30.7 years, its 135 scrolls and its 79%. Checked 2026-10-31 against the Revelation First census record of 2026-10-30 and the sources it saved.
  • COPIES KEPT APART FROM COMPOSITIONS. 'Some copies appear closer in time to their presumed historical authors'. The record's negative tag is that the model dates copies; the composition keeps the distinction in its own words. This is the distinction the field turns on.
  • THE FINDING ENLARGED. 'Enoch indicates that a significant portion of the scrolls are 50 to 150 years older than traditional paleographic estimates.' The study: 'often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates'. The range and the 'significant portion' are not in the saved sources.
  • TWO RESULTS MADE ONE. 'The Daniel fragment (`4Q114`) and Ecclesiastes manuscript (`4Q109`) were backdated substantially'. The study separates them: 'this study’s 14 C result for 4Q114 and Enoch’s date prediction for 4Q109 now establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors'. The Daniel date is the radiocarbon result (230–160 BCE); only Ecclesiastes is the model's. The figures 'from 175–150 BCE to roughly 300–250 BCE' are not in the saved sources, which give Enoch's 4Q109 prediction as 'a third-century BCE date'.
  • THE STATED LIMIT, ELSEWHERE. The study names its problem, 'an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts'. The composition gives doubt through Reddit ('carbon-dating uncertainties') and Popović's caution through Haaretz; the study's own limit is unsaid.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

A machine-dating study is composed nearly at its own grain, and it carries the distinction between when a text was copied and when it was written. Its figures grow where the press rounded them, and its doubts are sourced to a forum.

Inline links are Google redirect URLs, kept as pasted.] [QUERENT] Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls [SYSTEM] Researchers at the University of Groningen developed an artificial intelligence model named [Enoch](https://www.google.com/search?q=Enoch) to re-date the [Dead Sea Scrolls](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fg%2F121sxbzn&q=Dead+Sea+Scrolls). [1] How Enoch Works * Training Data: The model was trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples from four Judean Desert sites. [[1], [2]] * Methodology: It combines Bayesian ridge regression, radiocarbon dating, and machine-learning handwriting analysis (evaluating angular and allographic stroke geometries from manuscript images without reading the text itself). [[1], [2]] * Accuracy: Enoch predicts dates with a mean absolute error of roughly 28 to 31 years, and 79% of its estimates for 135 undated scrolls aligned realistically with human paleographic evaluations. [[1], [2], [3]] Key Findings * Older Timelines: Enoch indicates that a significant portion of the scrolls are 50 to 150 years older than traditional paleographic estimates. [1] * Specific Texts: * The Daniel fragment (`4Q114`) and Ecclesiastes manuscript (`4Q109`) were backdated substantially—with Ecclesiastes potentially pushed back from 175–150 BCE to roughly 300–250 BCE. * Some copies appear closer in time to their presumed historical authors or predate major periods like the Hasmonean kingdom expansion and the Qumran settlement. [[1], [2], [3]] Scholarly and Community Reaction * Support: Supporters view Enoch as an objective "time machine" that injects quantifiable error margins into handwriting analysis. * Skepticism: On platforms like [Reddit](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqAEB6zswFUSI1o9h3UO3PlMOLJtiZcSIGt6bjfIEXpeE2WENSYUxnqNQKM9qb_dj0GigjAYBWw8MAcGhmMQeqElwazQOsf3Hjtcfp6Y1I4-u5VC87N59p8-xTQASf7TVc3sN2KvkKdTw7tAyQnJ3HZJeceKZdbTcItMkZEuetZBTDl3Ks5_4dhLgqv8aGzEnQSgXRWn_2GRiJalt5D4r2UMiNiLD4ep4b48), opinions are mixed, with some researchers and users raising caution over black-box AI models, carbon-dating uncertainties, and traditional historical assumptions. [[1], [2], [3]] Opinions on the reliability and implications of AI-driven dating for ancient manuscripts vary among researchers and the public. “More research is needed to understand how Enoch's work will affect our understanding of the chronology of the Dead Sea Scrolls, Popovic cautions.” [Haaretz](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAES2QEB6zswFeSBxaD4RVuTUGo-tpMbFqkcWEZV8_0Bjpaa3DxXXVLeUnOoh1yK23IsrAMC7gJAICaOyhyi_7e3fzOqF7uiCcSTpSmsdiZBcxiD8RgM-8uutlBpgkB7ef4DF3tjnsLSboxT2lEup2I3zvmMJZH6iCeBMGQBlalByADn308x6SkjedmE7avTGX4o-xgpIVDvmW3XTVUE0ZfFoBLRjVi2A1LDcEB5b8L2wiimFIMTpL1aDEBMBpn0h8Rax5BaryTiRHLz1VHbDLJO1nd5CqioBdhPUxPk) Would you like to explore how radiocarbon dating works for ancient parchment, or look into specific texts like the Book of Daniel fragments?
